item.title: OS AI Agent - v1.1.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
* Security: Built with Go 1.27.3, which refuses server certificates issued by eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities revoked for a key compromise * Set `context_window` on every provider to the context length its model is loaded with. The agent now starts summarizing older tool results as a conversation nears it, and sizes the default reply length from it on Anthropic providers and for Claude 4 and later models on Bedrock. Without it, providers on Anthropic's own API and Claude models on Bedrock count as 200,000 tokens and every other provider as 32,768, so a model loaded with less can run out of context * Bug fix: Long investigations re-ran their own searches and could spend their budget without writing an answer, because older tool results were hidden from the model after two rounds. Tool results are now sent in full until the conversation nears the provider's context window, then summarized with the values the agent used * Bug fix: Long answers stopped mid-sentence on Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 through the Anthropic provider, and on Claude 4 and later models on Bedrock, because thinking counts against the 4,096-token default reply length. The default is now 32,000 tokens, or a quarter of the provider's context window when that is under 128,000 tokens, and `default_max_tokens` still overrides it; set it for a Bedrock application inference profile, which keeps Bedrock's default. An answer cut off at that limit, at the model's context window, or by the provider's `request_timeout` while it is being written is kept, says which, and is recorded as truncated in the activity trail; one cut off by the timeout used to fail the turn * Bug fix: One request could make more than a thousand model calls over about an hour, because its limit of 128 calls started again each time a long request continued in the background. The limit now covers the whole request, with one call more only when the background time budget interrupts the last, and that last call writes an answer from what was found so far, saying it was cut short, instead of the request failing with none; an investigation stopped this way writes no decision event, as before * Bug fix: In one investigation the agent could run the same search many times over, each time costing a search. A call identical to an earlier successful one in the same request now gets that result back without running again, the chat marks its card as a repeat, and after three rounds of nothing but repeats the agent is asked for its answer * Bug fix: The Bedrock model list offered base model IDs that Bedrock refuses for current Claude models; it now offers their inference profiles, such as `global.` and `us.`. The docs name the IAM permissions a Bedrock provider needs, including `bedrock:CallWithBearerToken` for a Bedrock API key and `bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles` for the model list * Bug fix: A date given to the agent, such as the "observed 2025-08-01 to 2025-08-14" of a threat report, was refused by Splunk as a search time bound, and the agent searched the last 24 hours instead. A date, a date-time with or without an offset, and Splunk's MM/DD/YYYY now work as `earliest` and `latest`, in the user's Splunk timezone, with `latest` on a date including that whole day * Bug fix: The agent took "now" in the search head's timezone, usually UTC, while Splunk shows each user search results in their own timezone, so it misread the times in results and shifted its relative time ranges by the difference. It now uses the user's Splunk timezone preference (the run-as user's in an alert investigation or `| osai task=`), and the search head's when the user has set none


Short Description:
Bring your own LLM to Splunk. OS AI Agent runs inside Splunk with OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, DeepSeek or a local model: ask in plain English and it searches your data, writes and verifies SPL, builds dashboards and alerts once you approve them, and investigates alerts on its own, read-only, always within each user's Splunk permissions.


Description:
OS AI Agent is an AI assistant that runs inside Splunk, with the model you choose. Point it at the provider you already pay for, or at a model on your own hardware, and ask in plain English: it explores your indexes, writes and verifies SPL, shows every search it ran, and answers with the numbers. Bring your own model. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OpenAI, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Groq, and local servers such as LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM or llama.cpp), Anthropic, Azure OpenAI and AWS Bedrock, with retries, failover between providers, prompt caching and Splunk's proxy settings. A local model on your laptop costs nothing per question. It builds, with your approval. Ask for a Dashboard Studio dashboard, a report or an alert. In Chat, anything that writes pauses on an approval card that shows exactly what will be created; approve it, deny it with a reason, or edit it first. It investigates when you are not watching. The "Ask OS AI Agent" alert action and the `| osai` command run read-only investigations from alerts and scheduled searches, and can record a decision, from answers you define, as an event your next alert can act on. **It knows your deployment.** It reads your macros, lookups, data models and installed commands as the signed-in user, follows your query templates and situational guidance, and uses the add-on commands an administrator allows, such as Kubernetes Search or Search for AWS, for data that is in no index. It runs as you. Every tool runs with the calling user's own Splunk permissions, provider keys stay in Splunk's credential store, and an activity trail records every turn, tool call, refusal and configuration change. Token Usage, Activity Trail and Health dashboards show cost per user and provider, what the agent did, and how it is running. Spend limits and a concurrency cap keep a budget a budget. Free to start. The free tier runs one provider for one user, for non-commercial use, with no license key. A license, priced per user, lifts both limits. Works on Splunk Enterprise 9.4, 10.0, 10.2, 10.4 and 10.6 and on Splunk Cloud, on a search head with KV Store, including search head clusters. The app sends no telemetry. Documentation: https://www.outcoldsolutions.com/docs/ai-agent/

Enrich the SHA-1 file hashes already in your Splunk environment with NetClean’s verified risk intelligence on human insider risk, a specialized area within insider risk. Description:
The ProActive File Analysis Connector for Splunk enriches the SHA-1 file hashes already in your Splunk environment with NetClean’s verified risk intelligence on human insider risk, a specialized area within insider risk. The connector submits the hashes to the ProActive File Analysis API and stores the result in Splunk together with contextual metadata, ready to use in your searches, alerts, dashboards and response workflows. A match means that a file corresponds to a risk indicator verified by trusted sources. It is a verified event, not a heuristic alert, and gives your insider risk program a high-confidence insider risk signal that calls for investigation. A match describes the content, not the person, so an investigation is always needed to understand the situation. A built-in alert and dashboard are included, and the connector works with the data and tools you already run.

item.title: Data Migration Toolkit for Splunk - v0.7.2 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Fixes from a real Windows to Linux move into AWS. * Import checks that it can write to the staging folder before it places anything, and prints the fix if not. * The plan uses the target’s Splunk version and free disk from target discovery, and warns when the typed version differs. Test connection fills in the target version. * A target indexer entered as its IP or management address matches the server found by discovery. * The run steps on the Setup and run page show real paths, systemctl where systemd runs Splunk, ownership of the staging folder, a dry run before import, and PowerShell commands for Windows sources. * Empty staging folders default to C:\smig\_staging or /opt/smig\_staging. * Discovery records whether systemd runs Splunk and which user Splunk runs as.


Short Description:
Move Splunk index data between deployments and prove nothing was lost. Windows to Linux, single instance or distributed to an indexer cluster, cluster to cluster, and several deployments into one. Read only discovery, a bucket by bucket plan, checksummed copies, and per index validation.


Description:
Moving indexed data from one Splunk deployment to another is usually a long, manual, error prone job: copying buckets by hand, renaming them for a cluster, fixing Windows paths, guessing at disk space, and hoping the counts match afterwards. Data Migration Toolkit for Splunk automates that work and shows you every step before anything moves. Supported paths: * Windows to Linux, in any topology * Single instance or distributed indexers to an indexer cluster * Indexer cluster to a single instance or to non clustered indexers * Indexer cluster to indexer cluster, including into a cluster that already holds data * Several deployments merged into one target * Like for like moves to new hardware or a new data center How it works: 1. Discover: read only REST and search queries inventory indexes, buckets, versions, sizes and readiness problems (index names Linux will not accept, missing journals, Windows paths in configuration, SmartStore, corrupt buckets). 2. Plan: a dry run report shows where every bucket goes, its new name, capacity per target indexer, size limit checks, the generated indexes.conf, and a runbook with the exact command for each host. Nothing moves until you approve it. 3. Copy: export and import are resumable, check a SHA256 for every bucket, never overwrite anything on the target, and never change the source except rolling hot buckets at cutover. 4. Validate: event counts per index per UTC day are compared on both sides, with an HTML report you can hand to the change approver. Dashboards on the target show live progress per plan, index and host. The source stays intact, so rollback is pointing forwarders back at it. A free browser based planner at augustschell.com builds the same plan from a discovery manifest, without uploading it. Not supported: SmartStore indexes and Splunk Cloud as a source or target. Free, by August Schell. Licensed under Apache 2.0.

1.2.1: Initial Splunkbase release. * IEV Overview, Opportunities, History, and Settings and About dashboards. * Eligible sourcetype lookup built from the Splunk IEV documentation (10.6). * Three data source modes: license usage, event estimate (tstats counts times sampled event size) and auto, plus an optional demo mode with synthetic data. * History and event size profile stored in KV store, so they survive app upgrades. * Settings stored as search macros, editable by admin or sc\_admin. * Search time only: no Python, custom JavaScript, modular inputs, data models or external calls. Splunk Cloud compatible.


Short Description:
See how much of your Splunk ingest is IEV eligible Cisco data, your effective license consumption at the 0.5x weight, and Cisco data on ineligible sourcetypes.


Description:
IEV Evaluation by August Schell shows what Splunk Integrated Enterprise Value (IEV) for Cisco data is worth in your environment. Under IEV, eligible Cisco data ingested with a supported sourcetype counts at a 0.5x weight against applicable ingest entitlement. Most organizations do not know how much of their ingest qualifies. This app measures it. The app matches your ingest by sourcetype against the list of IEV eligible sourcetypes published by Splunk, then shows actual ingest, eligible Cisco ingest, effective license consumption and estimated savings. It also finds Cisco data that is not landing on an eligible sourcetype, so you can see value being left on the table before your renewal. Volume can come from license usage (license_usage.log), from an estimate based on tstats event counts and sampled event sizes when license data is not visible, or from built in demo data. The app runs entirely at search time with no Python, custom JavaScript, modular inputs, data models or external network calls, so it works in air gapped and FIPS environments and in Splunk Cloud Platform. Results are estimates for planning. Splunk validates eligible usage and determines actual IEV treatment under your order and applicable terms.

item.title: Nikhil Chawla Add-on for Cisco Secure Firewall eStreamer (FMC) - v2.1.3 [New App Release]
item.description:

Release Notes:
2.1.3 - first release on Splunkbase \- Collects Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) connection events over eStreamer as sourcetype cisco:sfw:estreamer, with the field names the Cisco Security Cloud app uses \- Built-in eStreamer decoder, Python standard library only; reads connection data blocks 160 to 174 (FMC 6.x and 7.x) \- Inputs page for inputs and client certificates (PKCS12 or PEM, stored encrypted in Splunk's credential store), and a Status dashboard \- Policy names: FirewallPolicy, PrefilterPolicy and TunnelRule \- Resumes from a bookmark after restarts; disk buffer with a size cap; files are deleted once Splunk has read them


Short Description:
High-volume collector for Cisco Secure Firewall (FMC) connection events over eStreamer. Indexes them as cisco:sfw:estreamer with the Cisco Security Cloud app's field names, so its CIM mappings and dashboards work. Inputs, certificates and status are managed in Splunk Web. Independent project, not affiliated with Cisco.


Description:
Collects connection events from a Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) over eStreamer and indexes them as sourcetype cisco:sfw:estreamer, with the field names the Cisco Security Cloud app uses for that sourcetype (InitiatorIP, ResponderIP, FirewallRule, AC_RuleAction, ...). That app's field aliases, CIM mappings and dashboards therefore work on these events, and existing searches keep working. Busy FMCs send thousands of connection events per second. This add-on is built for that volume: each input decodes in parallel processes, keeps events on disk until Splunk has read them, and resumes from a bookmark after a restart, so a restart does not skip events. - One input per FMC, several FMCs per heavy forwarder - Inputs page in Splunk Web: add, edit, enable, disable and restart inputs, and upload the eStreamer client certificate (the PKCS12 file from the FMC, or PEM). Certificates are stored encrypted in Splunk's credential store. - Status dashboard: throughput, minutes behind the FMC, connects and errors, indexed volume and index delay per FMC - Names from the FMC's metadata: rules, access control policy (FirewallPolicy), prefilter policy (PrefilterPolicy), tunnel/prefilter rule (TunnelRule), zones, interfaces, devices, applications, URL categories and countries - host is a name you choose for each FMC; the FMC's address is in every event as SourceHost - Disk buffer with a size cap: files are deleted once Splunk has read them; when the buffer is full, delete the oldest files or pause - Python standard library only, no third-party packages Connection events only. Intrusion, file/malware and packet events can come from the Cisco Security Cloud app. Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Cisco. Cisco, Cisco Secure Firewall, Firepower and FMC are trademarks of Cisco Systems, Inc.

Short Description:
Send Splunk the logs that sampling and filters keep out to fit the license, on that same license. Compact events take a fraction of the volume and expand back byte-identical at search time; classic dashboards keep their SPL, and one command covers the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API.


Description:
With the Log10x App, Splunk can index compact log events and still search, chart and alert on the original lines. The 10x Receiver stores each event as a template hash plus the values that change, so a stream of repeated patterns takes less of the license. On the OpenTelemetry demo, Splunk's license meter counted 63.91% fewer bytes, encoded events and templates included, and every line expanded back byte-identical with the Receiver settings in the installation steps (measurement: https://github.com/log-10x/benchmarks/tree/main/splunk-license). The same license then holds more: sources that were sampled, filtered or kept out of Splunk to stay under the limit can come back, or the license can be smaller. Classic dashboards keep their SPL: the browser sends each panel's search to the app, which rewrites it on the server. From the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API, a search is wrapped in the tx command (tenxsearch also works). An alert created in the app's Compile Alert view is compiled once into a native saved search, so the scheduler runs no Python. NOT, OR, groups, phrases, field conditions, and values such as IP addresses and hostnames behave as they do on the original data. The 10x Receiver produces compact events, and it is free on up to 10 nodes (https://www.log10x.com/pricing). No sign-up is required to evaluate it: with no license token it runs the full product for 30 days on up to 10 nodes, air-gapped, and a free license removes the time limit (https://doc.log10x.com/manage/license/). The app itself is open source under the MIT license.

item.description:

Release Notes:
Version 1.4.0 carries the 1.3.0 changes as well, which were never published separately, so an upgrade from 1.2.1 lands both sets at once. NEW: three saved searches an AI agent can call by name. PolySwarm Indicator Lookup takes one indicator and returns one row. PolySwarm Indicator Lookup with Attribution adds malware family and actor at up to double the cost. PolySwarm Quota Remaining reports what is left and spends no indicator quota. They exist so an AI agent reaching Splunk through an MCP server can use this app without an administrator registering a custom tool or editing an allowlist. All three ship disabled. Two of them spend a metered request every time something dispatches them, so turning them on is a deliberate act: Settings, Searches reports and alerts, with the App filter and the Owner filter both set to All, then Enable from the row's Edit menu. They carry no schedule, so enabling one starts nothing. NEW FIELD: polyswarm_status, on both lookup searches, reading answered, not_found, refused or error. A lookup that failed used to be indistinguishable from a value PolySwarm has no record of. It is not any more. NEW FIELD: daily_api_metered, on the account row. An unmetered plan reports a daily limit of zero beside a remaining count that reads as nothing left and means no cap. This field says which it is. FIXED: the command now reads its credential and its configuration in this app's namespace. Running polyswarmsearch from another app, the Search app included, failed with an error saying no API key was stored. That is the first thing many customers tried. FIXED: a missing API key reported a Python file path and a line number. Every command now names the setup page instead. CHANGED, AND IT CHANGES A PUBLISHED FIELD: PolyScore is no longer published for a URL, a domain or an address. The column is still there and it is empty on those rows. The platform returns the same score for every URL artifact whatever the detection engines reported, so a convicted host read as benign. Read the verdict and the detection counts for those indicator types. If you alert, rank or report on PolyScore for URL, domain or address indicators, review those rules before upgrading. CHANGED: certificate verification on the app's connection to splunkd is now an administrator setting, and it ships off. Splunk ships an environment variable that disables verification outright, so the setting makes the choice visible rather than assumed. RENAMED: the app is now PolySwarm Malware Reputation and Sandbox. The app id, the directory, every command, every field name and every saved object are unchanged, so an upgrade carries everything over. Tested on Splunk Enterprise 10.6.0.5. Supported on 9.4 through 10.6 and on Splunk Cloud Platform.


Short Description:
PolySwarm malware reputation, sandbox detonation and file reputation for Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud. Hash lookup and IOC enrichment for MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, URLs, domains and IP addresses: crowd-sourced verdicts from many engines, malware family attribution, an opt-in threat intel feed, a matching search and three saved searches an AI agent can call.


Description:
PolySwarm Malware Reputation and Sandbox integrates crowd-sourced malware threat intelligence into Splunk by enriching indicators of compromise, or IOCs, with verdicts derived from multiple detection engines. It is a file reputation and hash lookup source for the SOC: the app processes MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, URLs, domains and IP addresses found in Splunk events, annotating them with verdicts, detection counts and malware family attribution sourced from the PolySwarm platform. It extracts and refangs indicators from raw text fields within the search head environment, at no cost and with no API key, and submits URLs to a cloud-based sandbox for behavioral analysis. The app operates entirely on the search head tier and relies on a key-value store to cache verdict data, track sandbox task state, and maintain modular input checkpoints. Enrichment occurs through five specialized search commands that query the PolySwarm API: the indicators being looked up are sent to PolySwarm, and nothing else from the deployment is transmitted. A local verdict cache means a repeated indicator costs nothing, and every metered request carries an explicit ceiling. Search heads that reach the internet through a proxy can route this traffic through it, with credentials held in encrypted storage and certificate verification on the PolySwarm connection always enforced. Events tagged with the polyswarm:artifact source type represent threat intel pulled from the PolySwarm feed and from sandbox task results, and each one carries the artifact's MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 so it can be matched against events however your own sources log a digest. Four saved searches ship and all four ship disabled. PolySwarm Indicator Match correlates the indexed feed against your own events and carries the verdict, detection counts, family attribution and report link through to the alert, so an analyst sees why a match matters rather than only that one occurred; it reads indexed events only and spends no PolySwarm quota. The other three are for an AI agent reaching Splunk through an MCP server: PolySwarm Indicator Lookup answers for one indicator, the same search with Attribution adds family and actor, and PolySwarm Quota Remaining reports what is left without spending indicator quota. Two of those three spend a metered request per run, which is why enabling them is a deliberate administrative act. Every answer carries a status field reading answered, not_found, refused or error, so an automated caller never has to read English to learn whether a lookup failed or the platform holds no record. Three dashboards cover enrichment activity and entitlement, sandbox detonations, and per-indicator triage. Opening any of them spends nothing. Four workflow actions give an analyst one-click enrichment from a search result's field menu, enrichment with attribution, navigation to the PolySwarm portal, and the triage page opened on that indicator.

Query your Kubernetes clusters live from the Splunk search bar - like kubectl, as SPL. List resources, stream pod logs, read events, and describe objects across every registered cluster. Description:
Kubernetes Search brings live, read-only access to the Kubernetes API into the Splunk search bar. Instead of switching to a terminal and kubectl, you run SPL - | k8s kind=pods namespace=payments - and Splunk queries the cluster's API server directly and streams the current state into your search. The problem it solves: when something breaks in a cluster, the question is usually "what is true right now?" - is the pod still crash-looping, what do its events say, is the node Ready. Answering that has meant leaving Splunk, holding cluster credentials, and running kubectl by hand. Ingestion pipelines give you history, but at the cost of storage and license volume, and they show the cluster only as of the last sample. Kubernetes Search answers the live question from inside Splunk, with no credentials handed out and every query recorded in the Splunk audit log. How it works: - Five search commands cover the common kubectl verbs: | k8s (list or get any resource), | k8slogs (stream pod logs), | k8sevents (cluster events), | k8sdescribe (an object plus its events), and | k8syaml (format JSON as YAML). - Everything runs on the search head and is strictly read-only - it never applies, scales, or deletes anything. - Nothing is indexed: no storage cost, no license volume, no source types, no field extractions. Results exist only for the life of your search. - Register many clusters and fan out with context=* - each row carries a cluster field, so you query and aggregate across your whole fleet from one pane. - Access is gated by a Splunk capability and a per-cluster credential model (shared, per-user, or Kubernetes impersonation), so analysts get controlled, audited read access without being handed kubectl or cluster credentials. - A short-lived on-disk cache keeps dashboards from hammering your API servers; Secrets are never cached. There is no agent to install in your cluster - only a network route from the search head to the API server and a credential. The app installs on search heads only and writes nothing to any index. It pairs naturally with ingestion: use Monitoring Kubernetes or OpenTelemetry for history and trends, and Kubernetes Search for the live picture - in the same Splunk session. Kubernetes Search runs on a free tier with no license key (one user and one cluster, on a single standalone search head). A paid license, priced per user, covers your whole team and unlocks multiple clusters, search head clustering, per-user credentials, and impersonation. Built and supported by Outcold Solutions. Description:
Dashboard Studio has no built-in clock, yet operations walls, NOC status boards, world-clock panels and "as of now" headers all want a live, ticking time display. **Realtime Clock** adds two purpose-built custom visualizations that render the current time entirely client-side at 60fps — no streaming data, no scheduled searches, no backend. **Analog Clock** — a smooth analog face with sweeping hands, tick marks, an optional digital readout and day/date line, and a configurable phosphor glow. Hand, second-hand and tick colours are all configurable. **Digital Clock** — a seven-segment LCD-style display with a blinking colon, 12/24-hour modes, optional seconds, a date line, ghost (unlit) segments for an authentic LCD look, and a phosphor glow. Both support **local time, UTC, or any IANA timezone** (e.g. `Europe/London`, `America/New_York`, `Asia/Tokyo`), so a single dashboard can show a row of world clocks. item.title: Cisco CDR Reporting and Analytics - v9.0.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
- **Important** - CUBE legs now join the CUCM legs of the same call only when "merge by ciscoguid" is selected on Investigate > Calls. The old automatic join on the first 8 characters of the guid is gone. - **Important** - This app no longer contains any CUBE configuration. For CUBE data install SA_cube 0.8.0 on the search head and TA_cube 0.8.0 on the indexers. - Removed the old hidden guids and guid_detail views. The guid diagnostics page no longer reports on call_reference_id. - call_reference_id, incoming_call_reference_id and outgoing_call_reference_id are deprecated and no longer used by the app. They are still extracted so saved searches keep working, and will be removed in a future release. - **Functionality** - Major improvements to the conversationId chaining feature. The prior implementation only performed a partial join in some cases. - Merging on Investigate > Calls is now done by a new mergecalls search command, which merges whole calls, follows chains of linked calls of any length, and holds only a few hours of calls in memory at a time. - **Functionality** - New "merge across SME by session id" option on Investigate > Calls (experimental), which joins the legs of a call on either side of an SME by their RFC 7989 session ID. - **Functionality** - New "merge by ciscoguid" option on Investigate > Calls. Unlike the conversationId and session id options it is not CUCM-only: ciscoguid means the same thing on CUCM, CUBE, CVP and SBC records, so it merges a call across clusters and across technologies. - **Functionality** - In all versions of Investigate Calls prior to this release the concurrency and duration_elapsed fields were always empty for every data type except CUCM and CUBE. Both now work for all of them. - **Performance** - The Investigate > Devices page is dramatically faster, commonly 5x to 10x, and more on larger deployments, as a result of eliminating an mvexpand in the SPL. - **Performance** - Investigate > Calls, and every other search that uses the devices lookup, is commonly 2x faster or more, because that lookup no longer allows wildcards. - **Important** - A "*" in the clusterId column of the devices lookup no longer matches any cluster. A new health check lists such rows, and the new App Settings > General page can turn wildcards back on. - **Important** - A CUCM node that is upgraded or reinstalled can reuse old call ids, merging unrelated calls. A new health check finds this, and the new call_id_resets lookup keeps them apart. Each warning includes a search you can run once to record the reset. - On Investigate > Calls, legs of one call that connect in the same second are now always listed in origination order, rather than sometimes in arbitrary order. - On Investigate > Calls, a leg with no value in a text column, or in duration, no longer shifts the values below it up a row, against the wrong leg. This was most common on calls that cross CUCM, CUBE, Oracle SBC and CVP. Other numeric columns, and the CMR quality columns, are not lined up with the legs yet. - **Functionality** - The field gallery now documents the Oracle SBC CDR fields, about 230 of them, so they appear in the field picker with descriptions when Oracle SBC is selected. It also fills in 50 CUBE fields that were missing. - The home page's Explore fields panel now samples CUBE and Oracle SBC data separately from CUCM, so their fields no longer show as not in your data. Each field now also says which data types it is found in, and the search box matches on that too. - Eleven fields are now treated as numbers rather than as categories, including the CUCM audio and video bandwidth fields, CUBE's h323_voice_quality and charged_units, and the CMR's videoOneWayDelay. - The Extension, Outside Party and Huntgroup detail pages no longer mix CUBE records into some of their panels. Those panels counted a call through both CUBE and CUCM twice and disagreed with the rest of the page. For CUBE, use Investigate > Calls. - The Call Detail page now labels legs from the cube_cdr_compact sourcetype with their CUBE direction and activity, as it already did for cube_cdr. - On Investigate > Calls, selecting some but not all clusters no longer hides every CUBE, Oracle SBC and CVP leg. The cluster filters now apply only to CUCM records. - **Functionality** - CVP calls now show on Investigate > Calls with CVP selected, one leg per SIP INVITE, and join their CUCM call under "merge by ciscoguid". Needs SA_cisco_ucce 0.2.0. - **Critical** - On a Splunk Free license the app's first-time-run script never ran at all, because Splunk cannot honor passAuth = splunk-system-user there. None of the app's editable lookups were ever created. - Expanded the field gallery descriptions for the directory URI party fields. - The gallery now also notes that a directory URI whose host is an IP address is the SIP URI as signaled, which incidentally is the same form Expressway, Cisco Meeting Server and SBC records use. - Expanded the gallery descriptions for the RFC 7989 session ID fields and the IMS charging fields (ICID and the IOI pair), which are purpose-built cross- system correlators rather than addresses. - Fixed a bug in the search filters field, where a tab character preceding a field=value searchterm would be handled incorrectly triggering a parse error from splunkd. - The callquality command no longer fails the entire search when call_quality_thresholds.csv is absent. It falls back to the shipped default thresholds and warns. - The two "Other calls to/from" panels on the CUBE call detail view now show whole calls, rather than only the legs that carried one of the parties, and no longer collapse identical legs into one. - Fixed a bug where the call detail page found no CUBE legs at all for a call whose guid begins with a zero, roughly one call in sixteen. It matched the zero-padded call_reference_id against the guid text, which is not padded. - The call detail page now finds a call's CUBE legs by ciscoguid. Before, a CUBE leg reached through a CUCM trunk-to-trunk leg was missing there, even when Investigate Calls showed it. - The call detail page has its own data type selector, set from Investigate Calls, and brings in a call's records from every selected system that carries its ciscoguid: CUBE, Oracle SBC, CVP, UCCE and CCCSP. - On Investigate Calls, a call that went through CUCM and an Oracle SBC now has one "view call details" link, to the main call detail page, as CUBE calls already did. The Oracle SBC detail view remains for calls that never touched CUCM. - The call flow diagram on the call detail page now draws a call's Oracle SBC and CUBE hops alongside its CUCM legs, with each box named the way it is named in CUCM. - In the call detail page's legs table, every non-CUCM row now gets the alternate background, the note above the table names which systems those rows came from, and data_type is now a default column. - The "other data sources" panel on the call detail page now also searches the app's own indexes, and recognizes a call's ciscoguid in each of the forms those systems write it. - Fixed a bug where if you had the conversationId merging option on, CUBE and Cisco Meeting Server legs fell out of any call that merged, and showed up as a separate call carrying a CUCM call id. - The health checks for required Splunk and app versions are now one check each, covering every installed Sideview app, in place of the eight near- identical copies the apps used to ship. Six fewer searches run when the health checks page loads. - Those two checks also now work for roles without the rest_access_server_endpoints capability, where previously they failed outright rather than reporting anything. - A sourcetypes list in sideview_data_types.conf may now be comma-separated as well as space-separated. Before, a comma silently hid that data type's events. - The devices lookup health check no longer fails when extra columns have been added to the lookup. Extra columns are now reported as INFO, and only missing columns fail the check. - The call_failed field no longer counts ordinary human outcomes as failures: wrong numbers (including SIP 404, 410, 484 and 604), no answer, busy (including SIP 486 and 600), declined (603), the caller hanging up while it rang (487), answered on another phone, or a party dropped from a conference. - Calls ending in SIP 420 Bad Extension or cause 155 "DCC Allowed Percentage Exceeded" previously had no call_failed value at all. Both now count as failed calls. - New fields connected_at and disconnected_at, defined the same way on every supported data type: when each call leg connected (empty if it never did) and when it ended. - Fixed duration_elapsed showing 0 for a call that did connect, when one of its CUCM legs never connected.


Description:
This commercial app is available as a 60 day trial and is compatible with both Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud. The app gives your team greatly increased visibility, monitoring, and reporting functionality around Cisco Unified Communications (aka CUCM / CallManager), whether you're a small organization with a hundred phones or one of the largest companies in the world. Whether troubleshooting individual calls or building high level reporting, it helps you visualize and understand in all areas: agents, users, and huntgroups; concurrency and utilization; call flow; call quality; call volume; devices; failed calls; locations and sites; and audits and compliance. item.description:

Release Notes:
To keep **searches responsive** over large modules (e.g. `logarchive`), the Addon extracts a selected set of high-value fields at **index time** for the `digit:saf:parseddata:json` source type only. These fields are stored in the index and and bring a massive performance gain when searching. The index-time fields are prefixed with `saf_idx_` (underscores only) so their names are unique, valid as indexed field keys, and never collide with the search-time `KV_MODE = json` fields. The original (un-prefixed, dotted) names remain available at search time via `KV_MODE = json`, but don't benefit from the speed. **For a given field you therefore have two names: use the `saf_idx_` name for fast filtering and `| tstats`, and the plain name (e.g. `data.process`) for everything else.** Indexed fields (12): `saf_idx_module`, `saf_idx_case_id`, `saf_idx_timestamp_desc`, `saf_idx_data_event_type`, `saf_idx_data_log_type`, `saf_idx_data_euid`, `saf_idx_data_boot_uuid`, `saf_idx_data_process`, `saf_idx_data_pid`, `saf_idx_data_subsystem`, `saf_idx_data_category`, `saf_idx_data_library`. Notes: * **Filtering** on an indexed field is faster transparently (e.g. `saf_idx_data_process=mussel`). **Aggregating** fast requires `| tstats` (e.g. `| tstats count by saf_idx_data_process`); a `search ... | stats` still scans raw events. Trailing wildcards (`keyword*`) use the index; leading wildcards (`*keyword`) do not. * Index-time fields apply only to data indexed **after** this config is in place. To benefit on existing cases, perform a one-time clean + reingest. New cases get the fields automatically. * **Scope:** because the indexed names carry the `saf_idx_` prefix, they are unique to this TA. `fields.conf` (`INDEXED = true`) applies only to these `saf_idx_*` names, so it does not affect the plain `KV_MODE = json` fields or any unrelated data on the same instance.


Description:

Cisco environments often produce data across multiple products, add-ons, indexes, sourcetypes, and data models. Building a consolidated view normally requires teams to create and maintain separate searches, dashboards, index mappings, and visualizations. This app provides a reusable foundation that brings those signals together through configurable dashboards, shared search definitions, index-mapping macros, health indicators, drilldowns, and interactive topology views. The app includes Secure Networking Posture dashboards covering Zero Trust Access, Secure Infrastructure, Scalable Network Segmentation, Hybrid Mesh Firewalling, and Agentic Operations. It also provides executive briefing, IT health, security, asset inventory, network readiness, building intelligence, Cisco Spaces, and network topology experiences. Searches use configurable index macros instead of hardcoded index names, allowing the app to adapt to different Splunk environments. Administrators can use the included Macro Index Tuning utility to discover relevant data and map dashboards to their indexes. Splunk App for Secure Networking does not collect Cisco data directly. It visualizes data already ingested into Splunk through applicable Cisco add-ons, integrations, and data models. The dashboards displayed and populated in each environment depend on the available data sources. The app is intended for network operations, security operations, IT operations, Splunk administrators, architects, customer success teams, and executives who need a consolidated view of the health, security, availability, and performance of their Cisco environment.
